description: Concept-first deck on distributed systems and data-intensive design: storage engines, replication, partitioning, transactions, consistency/CAP, consensus (Raft/Paxos), failure and time, streams, plus AWS/Azure/Kubernetes case studies. For cloud and platform architects.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::01 Foundations
notes.text: DDIA frames data systems by three concerns: {{c1::reliability}} (works correctly despite faults), {{c2::scalability}} (reasonable ways to cope with growing load) and {{c3::maintainability}} (people can keep working on it productively).

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::01 Foundations
notes.front: Fault vs failure: what's the difference?
notes.back: A fault is one component deviating from spec. A failure is the whole system no longer serving users. Fault tolerance = stopping faults from becoming failures.
notes.analogy: A flat tyre is a fault; being stranded on the motorway is a failure. A spare tyre is fault tolerance.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::01 Foundations
notes.front: Why measure response time with percentiles (p95, p99) rather than the mean?
notes.back: The mean hides the tail. Percentiles show how bad the slow requests are, and the slowest requests often belong to your heaviest, most valuable users.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::01 Foundations
notes.front: What is tail latency amplification?
notes.back: When one user request fans out to many backend calls, it is as slow as the slowest call, so even rare slow backends make many user requests slow.
notes.extra: Example: 100 parallel calls each with 1% chance of being slow → ~63% of requests hit at least one slow call.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::01 Foundations
notes.front: What are load parameters, and why do they matter for scalability?
notes.back: Numbers that describe your load: requests/sec, read/write ratio, cache hit rate, fan-out. There's no generically 'scalable' system; you design for a specific load profile.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::01 Foundations
notes.front: Scaling up vs scaling out?
notes.back: Scaling up: a bigger machine (vertical). Scaling out: more machines sharing the load, shared-nothing (horizontal).

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::02 Data Models & Storage Engines
notes.front: What is the object-relational impedance mismatch?
notes.back: The awkward translation between relational tables/rows and nested application objects. Document models (e.g. a résumé as one JSON tree) reduce it for self-contained, one-to-many data.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::02 Data Models & Storage Engines
notes.front: When do document models struggle and relational models win?
notes.back: When data has many many-to-many relationships or needs joins. Weak join support pushes join logic into app code; relational models handle it with foreign keys and joins.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::02 Data Models & Storage Engines
notes.front: Schema-on-write vs schema-on-read?
notes.back: Schema-on-write (relational): structure enforced when data is written. Schema-on-read (document): structure is implicit and interpreted by the reader; flexible, but readers carry the burden.
notes.analogy: Static vs dynamic typing: checked up front by the compiler, or discovered at run time by whoever uses the value.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::02 Data Models & Storage Engines
notes.front: Why does it matter that SQL is declarative?
notes.back: You say what you want, not how. The optimizer can change strategy (new indexes, parallel execution) without anyone rewriting queries.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::02 Data Models & Storage Engines
notes.text: Graph data models: the {{c1::property graph}} (vertices and edges with properties, queried with Cypher/Gremlin) and the {{c2::triple store}} (subject–predicate–object, queried with SPARQL). Both shine when many-to-many traversals dominate.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::02 Data Models & Storage Engines
notes.front: How does an LSM-tree storage engine handle a write?
notes.back: Append to a WAL, insert into an in-memory sorted memtable; when full, flush it as an immutable sorted file (SSTable). Background compaction merges SSTables, dropping overwritten/deleted keys.
notes.analogy: Like tossing notes into an inbox and filing them into sorted folders later, instead of finding the right page every time.
notes.extra: Examples: RocksDB, Cassandra, ScyllaDB, HBase; Kafka Streams state stores use RocksDB.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::02 Data Models & Storage Engines
notes.front: How does an LSM-tree answer a point read, and why can it be slow?
notes.back: Check the memtable, then SSTables newest to oldest. A key may need several files checked (read amplification); Bloom filters and sparse indexes skip most of them.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::02 Data Models & Storage Engines
notes.front: What is an SSTable, and why is the sorting useful?
notes.back: A Sorted String Table: key-value pairs sorted by key. Sorting allows mergesort-style compaction, a sparse in-memory index and efficient range scans.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::02 Data Models & Storage Engines
notes.front: Structurally, how do B-trees differ from LSM-trees?
notes.back: B-trees update fixed-size pages in place in a balanced tree. LSM-trees only append and later merge.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::02 Data Models & Storage Engines
notes.front: When does an LSM-tree beat a B-tree, and what does it cost?
notes.back: Write-heavy, time-series or wide-column workloads: sequential writes, higher throughput, better compression. Cost: compaction competes for I/O and reads/space amplify.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::02 Data Models & Storage Engines
notes.front: When does a B-tree beat an LSM-tree?
notes.back: Read-dominated, transactional workloads: predictable point/range reads, and each key lives in exactly one place, which makes locking simple (PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB).

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::02 Data Models & Storage Engines
notes.front: What is write amplification?
notes.back: Bytes physically written ÷ bytes logically written: one write triggers several disk writes (WAL, B-tree page splits, compaction rewrites). It limits write throughput and wears SSDs.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::02 Data Models & Storage Engines
notes.text: {{c1::Read amplification}}: disk reads (files/levels) needed per logical read. {{c2::Space amplification}}: bytes on disk ÷ bytes of live data (stale versions waiting for compaction).

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::02 Data Models & Storage Engines
notes.front: What does the RUM conjecture say about storage engines?
notes.back: No engine can minimize Read, Update (write) and Memory/space overhead at once. Tuning (e.g. compaction strategy) moves you around that triangle.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::02 Data Models & Storage Engines
notes.front: What does a Bloom filter do in an LSM store?
notes.back: A per-SSTable probabilistic set: 'definitely not here' or 'maybe here'. Point lookups skip files that can't hold the key. False positives possible, false negatives never.
notes.analogy: A bouncer with a guest list that sometimes waves in a stranger but never turns away an invited guest.
notes.extra: Costs a few bits per key of memory.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::02 Data Models & Storage Engines
notes.front: Why does almost every database keep a write-ahead log (WAL)?
notes.back: Durability: the change is appended and fsync'd to the log before the data structure is modified, so a crash can be recovered by replaying the log.
notes.extra: Cloud ops: WAL latency = commit latency, so put it on low-latency block storage (io2, Premium SSD v2), never object storage.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::02 Data Models & Storage Engines
notes.text: Besides crash recovery, the WAL feeds {{c1::physical replication}} (PostgreSQL streaming replication, MySQL binlog) and {{c2::change data capture}} tools such as Debezium.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::02 Data Models & Storage Engines
notes.front: OLTP vs OLAP workloads?
notes.back: OLTP: many small key-based reads/writes, latency-sensitive, user-facing, row-oriented. OLAP: few big queries scanning many rows but few columns, throughput-oriented, column-oriented warehouses.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::02 Data Models & Storage Engines
notes.front: Why is column-oriented storage good for analytics?
notes.back: Queries touch a few columns across millions of rows. Storing each column contiguously means reading only those columns, and similar adjacent values compress very well (bitmap, run-length).
notes.analogy: Reading only the 'price' column of a spreadsheet instead of every full row.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::02 Data Models & Storage Engines
notes.front: Why are writes expensive in a column store, and how do engines cope?
notes.back: One row insert touches every column file. Engines buffer writes (often in a row-oriented in-memory store) and append them in large sorted batches.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::03 Encoding & Schema Evolution
notes.text: {{c1::Backward}} compatibility: new code can read data written by old code. {{c2::Forward}} compatibility: old code can read data written by new code.
notes.extra: Rolling upgrades need both. Forward is harder: old code must ignore unknown fields.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::03 Encoding & Schema Evolution
notes.front: How do Protocol Buffers / Thrift keep schemas evolvable?
notes.back: Every field has a tag number. Add fields with new tags (old readers skip unknown tags); make new fields optional/defaulted (new readers handle old data). Never reuse a tag.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::03 Encoding & Schema Evolution
notes.front: How does Avro schema evolution differ from Protobuf/Thrift?
notes.back: No field tags. The writer's schema and reader's schema are resolved by field name at read time; only add/remove fields that have defaults.
notes.analogy: Two people with different forms for the same data line up the boxes by label, not by box number.
notes.extra: Good for generated schemas (e.g. from a DB table) and big files where the schema is stored once.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::04 Replication & Quorums
notes.text: Replication approaches: {{c1::single-leader}} (all writes go to one leader, followers copy), {{c2::multi-leader}} (several nodes accept writes, e.g. one per datacenter), {{c3::leaderless}} (clients write to several replicas directly, Dynamo-style).

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::04 Replication & Quorums
notes.front: Synchronous vs asynchronous replication: the trade-off?
notes.back: Sync: follower confirms before ack → guaranteed up-to-date copy, but a down follower blocks writes. Async: leader acks at once → fast and available, but a leader failure can lose recent writes.
notes.analogy: Sync is waiting for the signed delivery receipt; async is dropping the letter in the postbox and walking away.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::04 Replication & Quorums
notes.text: {{c1::Semi-synchronous}} replication: one follower is synchronous and the rest async, so at least two nodes always have every acknowledged write.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::04 Replication & Quorums
notes.front: What is replication lag, and what anomaly does it cause?
notes.back: The delay before an async follower catches up with the leader. Reads from that follower return stale data, which looks to users like lost or reordered writes.
notes.analogy: Like newspaper editions: a reader holding the morning print hasn't seen the afternoon correction yet.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::04 Replication & Quorums
notes.text: Session guarantees: {{c1::read-your-writes}} (you see your own writes), {{c2::monotonic reads}} (you never see time go backward), {{c3::monotonic writes}} (your writes apply in order), {{c4::writes-follow-reads}} (your write is ordered after what you read).

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::04 Replication & Quorums
notes.front: What do the four session guarantees add up to, and why are they worth providing?
notes.back: Causal consistency for a single client. They're cheap to provide, and most user-visible anomalies come from missing them.
notes.extra: K8s: passing resourceVersion gives writes-follow-reads.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::04 Replication & Quorums
notes.text: {{c1::Consistent prefix reads}}: if writes happen in a certain order, anyone reading them sees them in that order (no answer before its question).

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::04 Replication & Quorums
notes.text: Read-your-writes on an eventually consistent store: route reads to the {{c1::leader}}, carry a {{c2::version/session token}} the replica must have reached, or use {{c3::sticky routing}} to the replica you wrote to.
notes.extra: Costs: leader load, client complexity, lost load balancing. Examples: DynamoDB strongly consistent reads; Cosmos DB session token.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::04 Replication & Quorums
notes.front: In leaderless replication, what does w + r > n guarantee?
notes.back: The write set and read set overlap in at least one node, so a read sees at least one copy of the latest write.
notes.analogy: If 3 of 5 people heard the news and you ask any 3 of the 5, at least one of them heard it.
notes.extra: Pitfalls: sloppy quorums and concurrent writes can still break it.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::04 Replication & Quorums
notes.text: Leaderless repair: {{c1::read repair}} writes the fresh value back when a read sees a stale replica; {{c2::anti-entropy}} is a background process that compares and syncs replicas.
notes.extra: Read repair only fixes data that gets read; anti-entropy covers the rest.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::04 Replication & Quorums
notes.front: What is a sloppy quorum, and what does it cost?
notes.back: During a partition, writes are accepted on reachable nodes that aren't the key's 'home' nodes. Higher write availability, but w + r > n no longer guarantees reading the latest value.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::04 Replication & Quorums
notes.front: What is hinted handoff?
notes.back: After a sloppy-quorum write, the stand-in node forwards the write to the home node once it's reachable again.
notes.analogy: A neighbour takes in your parcel while you're away and hands it over when you're back.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::04 Replication & Quorums
notes.front: Leaderless concurrent writes: why prefer version vectors over last-write-wins?
notes.back: LWW picks the highest timestamp and silently discards the other write. Version vectors tell concurrent from causally ordered writes and keep both 'siblings' for the application to merge.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::04 Replication & Quorums
notes.text: Last-writer-wins converges trivially but has two failure modes: {{c1::silent data loss}} (one of two concurrent updates vanishes) and {{c2::clock dependence}} (a node with a fast clock wins even when its write is older).
notes.extra: Default in DynamoDB Global Tables and Cosmos DB multi-region writes. Use only where concurrent writes don't happen or don't matter.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::05 Partitioning
notes.front: Why partition (shard) data?
notes.back: To scale past one machine: spread data and query load over many shared-nothing nodes. Usually combined with replication, so each partition has copies on several nodes.
notes.analogy: Splitting a phone book into volumes A–F, G–M, … so several people can look things up at the same time.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::05 Partitioning
notes.front: Partition by key range vs by hash of key?
notes.back: Key range: keeps order, cheap range scans, but skewed access (e.g. timestamps) creates hot spots. Hash: spreads load evenly, but range queries must hit every partition.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::05 Partitioning
notes.front: Local vs global secondary indexes in a partitioned database?
notes.back: Local: each partition indexes its own rows; cheap writes, but reads scatter/gather to all partitions. Global: index partitioned by term; reads hit one partition, writes update remote index partitions (often async).

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::05 Partitioning
notes.front: Why avoid hash(key) mod N to assign partitions to nodes?
notes.back: Changing N moves almost every key. Instead use many fixed partitions spread over nodes, dynamic split/merge, or consistent hashing, so rebalancing moves only a fraction.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::05 Partitioning
notes.front: Why can one hot key throttle a DynamoDB/Cosmos DB table that has spare total capacity?
notes.back: Throughput is capped per physical partition, and one key always maps to one partition. A low-cardinality or time-clustered key concentrates load there.
notes.extra: Limits: DynamoDB ≈ 3,000 RCU / 1,000 WCU per partition; Cosmos DB 10,000 RU/s per physical partition, 20 GB per logical partition.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::05 Partitioning
notes.front: How do you fix a hot partition key?
notes.back: Choose a high-cardinality key, or write-shard it: add a random/hash suffix and scatter-gather on read. Also: pre-aggregate, cache (DAX), Cosmos DB hierarchical partition keys.
notes.extra: Same skill applies to Kafka partition keys.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::06 Transactions & Isolation
notes.text: ACID: {{c1::Atomicity}} (all-or-nothing), {{c2::Consistency}} (invariants preserved), {{c3::Isolation}} (concurrent transactions don't interfere), {{c4::Durability}} (committed data survives crashes).

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::06 Transactions & Isolation
notes.front: Which ACID property is mostly the application's job, and why?
notes.back: Consistency: the invariants are defined by your application. The database only provides atomicity and isolation so you can keep them.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::06 Transactions & Isolation
notes.front: What does read committed prevent, and what does it still allow?
notes.back: Prevents dirty reads (seeing uncommitted data) and dirty writes (overwriting uncommitted data). Still allows non-repeatable reads: re-reading a row can return a newer committed value.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::06 Transactions & Isolation
notes.front: What is snapshot isolation, and how is it implemented?
notes.back: Each transaction reads a consistent snapshot as of its start. Implemented with MVCC: keep several committed versions per row. Prevents non-repeatable reads.
notes.analogy: Each transaction reads from a photo of the database taken when it started, while others keep editing the real thing.
notes.extra: Often sold as 'repeatable read'.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::06 Transactions & Isolation
notes.front: What does MVCC cost operationally?
notes.back: Old row versions pile up until garbage collection (PostgreSQL VACUUM, InnoDB purge). Long-running transactions block cleanup → table bloat.
notes.extra: Managed services (Aurora, Azure Database for PostgreSQL) behave the same.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::06 Transactions & Isolation
notes.front: Lost update vs write skew?
notes.back: Lost update: two read-modify-write cycles on the same object; one overwrites the other. Write skew: two transactions read overlapping data, then update different objects, together breaking an invariant.
notes.extra: Snapshot isolation can prevent lost updates, but not write skew.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::06 Transactions & Isolation
notes.front: Give the canonical write skew example and the fixes.
notes.back: Two on-call doctors each see 2 on call and sign off concurrently; no row conflict, both commit → 0 on call. Fix: SERIALIZABLE (e.g. PostgreSQL SSI), SELECT … FOR UPDATE, or materialize the constraint as a row.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::06 Transactions & Isolation
notes.front: What is a phantom?
notes.back: A write in one transaction changes the result of a search query in another (rows appear/disappear). Row locks can't stop it; you need predicate or index-range locks.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::06 Transactions & Isolation
notes.text: Serializable isolation implementations: {{c1::actual serial execution}} (one thread, in memory, e.g. Redis, VoltDB); {{c2::two-phase locking (2PL)}} (readers and writers block each other; deadlocks); {{c3::serializable snapshot isolation (SSI)}} (optimistic, aborts conflicting transactions at commit).
notes.extra: 2PL is pessimistic (wait); SSI is optimistic (proceed, maybe abort).

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::07 Consistency Models & CAP
notes.front: Define linearizability.
notes.back: Every operation appears to take effect atomically at one instant between its invocation and response, in an order that respects real time. The system behaves like a single up-to-date copy.
notes.analogy: One shared whiteboard: once anyone has seen the new value, nobody can see the old one again.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::07 Consistency Models & CAP
notes.front: What scope does linearizability cover?
notes.back: A single object (one key, one register, one lock). It says nothing about multi-object transactions.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::07 Consistency Models & CAP
notes.front: Serializability vs linearizability?
notes.back: Serializability: multi-object transactions appear in some serial order, with no real-time constraint (may serve an old snapshot). Linearizability: single-object, real-time order.
notes.extra: 'Strongly consistent' in cloud docs usually means linearizable per key, not across keys.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::07 Consistency Models & CAP
notes.text: {{c1::Strict serializability}} = serializability + real-time order. Google Spanner calls it {{c2::external consistency}} and gets it from TrueTime commit-wait.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::07 Consistency Models & CAP
notes.front: Sequential consistency vs linearizability?
notes.back: Sequential: all clients see one total order that respects each client's program order, but not real time. A read may be stale, but never goes backwards.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::07 Consistency Models & CAP
notes.front: How does ZooKeeper give sequential rather than linearizable reads, and how do you upgrade a read?
notes.back: Writes go through the leader (linearizable); reads are served locally by any follower, so they can lag. Call sync() before the read to make it current.
notes.extra: The Kubernetes apiserver watch cache has the same shape.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::07 Consistency Models & CAP
notes.front: Causal order vs total order?
notes.back: Causal is a partial order: only events that could have influenced each other are ordered; concurrent ones aren't. Linearizability imposes a total order on everything.
notes.analogy: Nobody should see a reply before the question it answers, but two unrelated posts may appear in either order.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::07 Consistency Models & CAP
notes.front: Why is causal consistency the strongest model that stays available under partition?
notes.back: Causal dependencies can be tracked locally (vector clocks, dependency metadata). Ordering concurrent writes would need both sides of the partition to communicate.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::07 Consistency Models & CAP
notes.front: What does eventual consistency promise, and what does it not?
notes.back: Only that replicas converge if writes stop. It doesn't say when, what a read returns before then, that reads are monotonic, or which write wins.
notes.analogy: Village gossip: everyone eventually hears the same story, but at any moment people may tell different versions.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::07 Consistency Models & CAP
notes.front: What does eventual consistency need in order to actually converge?
notes.back: A deterministic merge rule: last-writer-wins, CRDTs, or version vectors plus an application merge. Without one you get divergence.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::07 Consistency Models & CAP
notes.front: State the CAP theorem precisely.
notes.back: During a network partition, a system cannot be both linearizable (C) and available (every non-failed node returns a non-error response) (A).
notes.analogy: Two bank branches with the phone line cut: refuse withdrawals (consistent) or allow them and risk an overdraft (available).
notes.extra: Says nothing about the no-partition case; PACELC fills that gap.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::07 Consistency Models & CAP
notes.front: Why is 'CAP: pick two of three' a misreading?
notes.back: Partitions aren't optional; they happen. The only choice is C vs A while partitioned.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::07 Consistency Models & CAP
notes.front: In CAP, what does the 'C' mean, and why does that matter?
notes.back: Linearizability specifically, not ACID consistency or 'any consistency'. A system can be causally consistent and still available.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::07 Consistency Models & CAP
notes.front: What does PACELC add to CAP?
notes.back: If Partitioned: A vs C; Else: Latency vs Consistency. Strong consistency costs latency even when nothing is broken.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::07 Consistency Models & CAP
notes.text: PACELC classes: etcd, ZooKeeper and Spanner are {{c1::PC/EC}}; DynamoDB (default) and Cassandra are {{c2::PA/EL}}; MongoDB with default concerns is {{c3::PA/EC}}.
notes.extra: Cosmos DB is configurable: strong/bounded ≈ PC/EC, session/eventual ≈ PA/EL.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::07 Consistency Models & CAP
notes.front: Why does strong consistency cost latency on a healthy network?
notes.back: A linearizable write must reach a majority before acking, and a linearizable read must confirm leadership or go to the leader: round trips on every request.
notes.extra: Numbers: cross-AZ RTT ~1–2 ms → quorum write ≈ 2–4 ms; cross-region 50–150 ms → Cosmos DB strong ≈ 2× RTT to farthest region.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::07 Consistency Models & CAP
notes.front: Heuristic: how do you decide CP vs AP for a piece of data?
notes.back: Ask: 'If two clients disagree about this value for a few seconds, what breaks?' Nothing (likes, presence, caches) → AP. Money, uniqueness, inventory, leadership → CP, or make the invariant monotonic.
notes.extra: Most systems mix a CP core (etcd, a ledger) with an AP periphery.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::07 Consistency Models & CAP
notes.front: Harvest vs yield (Fox & Brewer)?
notes.back: Yield: fraction of requests answered. Harvest: fraction of the data reflected in an answer. Under partial failure you choose which to degrade, e.g. answer from 9 of 10 shards.
notes.analogy: A search page that says 'some results may be missing' kept its yield by giving up some harvest.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::07 Consistency Models & CAP
notes.front: Why replace 'eventually consistent' with a number?
notes.back: Then the business can check whether it tolerates that staleness. E.g. DynamoDB eventual reads ≈ 1 s; Aurora replicas tens of ms; Azure GRS RPO < 15 min.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::07 Consistency Models & CAP
notes.front: Order by coordination needed: Raft write, CRDT increment, K8s pod creation, DynamoDB eventual read, S3 PUT.
notes.back: CRDT increment (none) → DynamoDB eventual read → S3 PUT (per-key metadata) → Raft write (majority + fsync) → pod creation (many sequential consensus writes).
notes.extra: Latency and availability ceilings follow this order.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::07 Consistency Models & CAP
notes.front: What does the CALM theorem say?
notes.back: Consistency As Logical Monotonicity: a program can be coordination-free and eventually consistent if and only if it is monotonic (outputs only grow: union, append, max).
notes.analogy: A guest list you can only add to: any order of additions gives the same final list, so nobody needs to coordinate.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::07 Consistency Models & CAP
notes.front: How do you use CALM as a design lever?
notes.back: Reformulate operations as monotonic (tombstones, CRDT counters, append-only logs) and reserve consensus for the remaining non-monotonic core (deletes, 'is this the only one?').

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::07 Consistency Models & CAP
notes.front: What does Jepsen test, and what's the recurring lesson?
notes.back: It runs concurrent clients against a real cluster while injecting partitions, clock skew and pauses, then checks the history. Lesson: 'strongly consistent' claims often fail only under partitions or leader changes.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::08 Consensus (Raft & Paxos)
notes.front: What problem does consensus solve?
notes.back: Getting N processes to agree on one value, or one ordered log, despite crashes and message delays.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::08 Consensus (Raft & Paxos)
notes.front: Why is consensus fundamentally hard?
notes.back: A slow node looks exactly like a dead one. A protocol must risk either waiting forever or acting on a false suspicion and deciding twice.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::08 Consensus (Raft & Paxos)
notes.front: What does the FLP result say?
notes.back: In a fully asynchronous system where even one node may crash, no deterministic consensus algorithm can guarantee it always terminates.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::08 Consensus (Raft & Paxos)
notes.front: How do Raft and Paxos coexist with FLP?
notes.back: They guarantee safety unconditionally, but liveness only under partial synchrony (timeouts eventually hold). Randomized timeouts make livelock improbable, not impossible.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::08 Consensus (Raft & Paxos)
notes.front: Why does tolerating f crash failures need 2f+1 nodes?
notes.back: Any two majorities of 2f+1 overlap in at least one node, which carries decisions across leader changes. With f down, f+1 (a majority) remain to make progress.
notes.analogy: Two majorities of the same committee always share at least one member, who remembers what the first one decided.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::08 Consensus (Raft & Paxos)
notes.front: Why does Byzantine fault tolerance need 3f+1 nodes?
notes.back: The overlapping nodes might lie, so quorums must overlap in f+1 nodes to guarantee at least one honest node in the intersection.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::08 Consensus (Raft & Paxos)
notes.front: Why is a quorum of 'any 2 of 5' unsafe for consensus?
notes.back: Two disjoint 2-node sets exist, so two leaders could commit different values at the same log index. Every write quorum must intersect every other.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::08 Consensus (Raft & Paxos)
notes.front: Flexible Paxos: which quorums must intersect, and what does that buy?
notes.back: Only phase-1 (election) and phase-2 (replication) quorums: |Q1| + |Q2| > N. Small Q2 gives fast steady-state commits; the bigger Q1 is paid only on leader change.
notes.extra: Same reasoning behind Aurora's 4/6 write, 3/6 read quorums.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::08 Consensus (Raft & Paxos)
notes.text: Raft splits consensus into {{c1::leader election}}, {{c2::log replication}} and {{c3::safety}}.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::08 Consensus (Raft & Paxos)
notes.front: What is Raft's State Machine Safety property?
notes.back: If any server has applied the entry at index i, no server will ever apply a different entry at i.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::08 Consensus (Raft & Paxos)
notes.front: What is a Raft term, and what does it solve without clocks?
notes.back: A monotonically increasing number with at most one leader per term. Every message carries it; higher term → step down, stale term → reject. Obsolete leaders are detected from message content alone.
notes.analogy: Like a dynasty number: an order sealed in a previous reign is void once a new ruler is crowned.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::08 Consensus (Raft & Paxos)
notes.front: Walk through a Raft leader election.
notes.back: A follower hears nothing for an election timeout → becomes candidate, increments term, votes for itself, sends RequestVote. Majority → leader, starts heartbeats. A valid leader's AppendEntries makes it step back.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::08 Consensus (Raft & Paxos)
notes.front: Why are Raft election timeouts randomized?
notes.back: So candidates rarely time out together; split votes resolve quickly. This is Raft's practical answer to FLP livelock.
notes.extra: Raft paper: 150–300 ms.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::08 Consensus (Raft & Paxos)
notes.front: Raft's election restriction: how is 'more up-to-date log' defined?
notes.back: Compare the last entries: higher term wins; same term → longer log wins. A voter refuses candidates less up-to-date than itself.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::08 Consensus (Raft & Paxos)
notes.front: What does Raft's election restriction guarantee, and how does that differ from Paxos?
notes.back: Leader Completeness: every committed entry is already in each new leader's log, so data only flows leader → follower. A new Paxos leader must first learn previously chosen values.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::08 Consensus (Raft & Paxos)
notes.front: State Raft's Log Matching Property.
notes.back: If two logs have an entry with the same index and term, the entries are identical and so are all entries before them.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::08 Consensus (Raft & Paxos)
notes.front: How does AppendEntries enforce Log Matching?
notes.back: Each RPC carries prevLogIndex/prevLogTerm. A follower rejects on mismatch; the leader backs up nextIndex until they agree, then overwrites the follower's divergent suffix.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::08 Consensus (Raft & Paxos)
notes.front: Why can't a Raft leader commit an old-term entry just by seeing it on a majority (Figure 8)?
notes.back: A later candidate whose last entry has a higher term can still win without that entry and overwrite it. Counting replicas is only safe for current-term entries.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::08 Consensus (Raft & Paxos)
notes.front: Why does a new Raft leader immediately append a no-op entry?
notes.back: Committing a current-term entry commits all earlier entries transitively, so the no-op makes previous-term entries committable at once.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::08 Consensus (Raft & Paxos)
notes.front: Why can't Raft switch membership straight from C<sub>old</sub> to C<sub>new</sub>?
notes.back: Servers adopt the change at different times, so a majority of Cold and a majority of Cnew could form two disjoint quorums in the same term.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::08 Consensus (Raft & Paxos)
notes.text: Safe Raft membership changes: {{c1::joint consensus}} (a transitional config needing majorities of both old and new) or {{c2::single-server changes}} (one at a time, so consecutive majorities always overlap; etcd's approach).

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::08 Consensus (Raft & Paxos)
notes.front: Why does etcd add new members as learners (non-voting) first?
notes.back: A fresh voter immediately enlarges the quorum while its log is empty, so 3→4 temporarily makes the cluster less available. Learners catch up first, then get promoted.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::08 Consensus (Raft & Paxos)
notes.front: Raft linearizable reads: ReadIndex vs lease-based?
notes.back: ReadIndex: confirm leadership with one heartbeat round, then serve once applied up to the commit index; costs a round trip, no clocks. Lease: no round trip, but correctness depends on bounded clock drift.
notes.extra: etcd defaults to ReadIndex.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::08 Consensus (Raft & Paxos)
notes.front: Without ReadIndex or leases, why can a Raft leader serve stale reads?
notes.back: A deposed leader cut off by a partition doesn't know a new leader exists and keeps answering from its old state.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::08 Consensus (Raft & Paxos)
notes.front: What are partial and asymmetric network partitions?
notes.back: Partial: A↔B and B↔C work but A↔C doesn't. Asymmetric: A can send to B but not receive from it. Real partitions are rarely a clean split.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::08 Consensus (Raft & Paxos)
notes.front: How does a partial partition make a Raft follower disruptive?
notes.back: It can't hear the leader, so it keeps starting elections with ever-higher terms. When it reconnects, its high term forces the healthy leader to step down, over and over.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::08 Consensus (Raft & Paxos)
notes.front: What does Raft PreVote do?
notes.back: Before an election, the candidate asks 'would you vote for me?' without bumping its term, and only proceeds if a majority agree. Stops cut-off followers from inflating terms.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::08 Consensus (Raft & Paxos)
notes.front: What does Raft CheckQuorum do?
notes.back: A leader that can't reach a majority within an election timeout steps down, so a partitioned leader stops serving (lease) reads.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::08 Consensus (Raft & Paxos)
notes.front: How does Raft log compaction (snapshotting) work?
notes.back: Each server snapshots its state machine up to a committed index and discards that log prefix, keeping the last included index/term and the membership config.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::08 Consensus (Raft & Paxos)
notes.front: What does a Raft leader do when a follower needs entries it already compacted?
notes.back: Sends InstallSnapshot. etcd also bootstraps new members this way.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::08 Consensus (Raft & Paxos)
notes.text: Paxos roles: the {{c1::proposer}} drives a ballot; the {{c2::acceptor}} votes and keeps the safety-critical state on stable storage; the {{c3::learner}} finds out which value was chosen.
notes.extra: In practice one process plays all three roles.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::08 Consensus (Raft & Paxos)
notes.front: Single-decree Paxos phase 1 (Prepare/Promise): what happens?
notes.back: The proposer sends Prepare(n) with a unique ballot n. Each acceptor promises to ignore ballots < n and returns the highest-ballot value it has already accepted, if any.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::08 Consensus (Raft & Paxos)
notes.front: Single-decree Paxos phase 2 (Accept): what happens?
notes.back: With a majority of promises, the proposer sends Accept(n, v), where v is the highest-ballot value returned (or its own if none). Accepted by a majority ⇒ chosen.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::08 Consensus (Raft & Paxos)
notes.front: Why must a Paxos proposer adopt the highest-ballot value returned in phase 1?
notes.back: Once v is chosen by majority M, any later phase-1 majority overlaps M and reports v, so every later ballot re-proposes v. Chosen values are sticky.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::08 Consensus (Raft & Paxos)
notes.front: How does Multi-Paxos amortize the protocol?
notes.back: Run phase 1 once to establish a stable leader over many log slots; each slot then needs only phase 2 (one round trip), the same steady-state cost as Raft.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::08 Consensus (Raft & Paxos)
notes.front: Multi-Paxos vs Raft: how do their logs differ?
notes.back: Paxos allows holes and out-of-order acceptance; a new leader must recover uncertain slots. Raft forces a contiguous log. Paxos is more flexible; Raft is easier to get right.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::08 Consensus (Raft & Paxos)
notes.front: What is the Paxos dueling proposers problem, and the fix?
notes.back: Two proposers keep issuing higher ballots, each invalidating the other's Accept → livelock. Fix: a distinguished leader and/or randomized backoff. A wrong leader guess costs liveness, never safety.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::08 Consensus (Raft & Paxos)
notes.front: What pattern do AWS's production Paxos uses (DynamoDB leader election, EBS, Route 53 ARC) share?
notes.back: Paxos guards a small, critical metadata/leadership plane; bulk data is replicated more cheaply (chain or quorum replication) under the elected leader.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::08 Consensus (Raft & Paxos)
notes.front: What is total order broadcast?
notes.back: Delivering messages reliably to all nodes in the same order. It's equivalent to consensus and underlies state machine replication: same ops, same order → same state.
notes.analogy: Every replica follows the same recipe card by card, so every kitchen ends up with the same dish.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::08 Consensus (Raft & Paxos)
notes.front: Why is two-phase commit (2PC) blocking?
notes.back: A participant that voted 'yes' must hold locks until the coordinator decides. If the coordinator crashes after prepare, participants are stuck: aborting alone is unsafe since it may have logged commit.
notes.analogy: An officiant asks both partners 'I do?', hears two yeses, then faints: the couple can neither leave nor call it off until he wakes.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::08 Consensus (Raft & Paxos)
notes.front: How does Spanner-style Paxos commit remove 2PC's blocking?
notes.back: The coordinator's decision is itself a consensus-replicated value (each participant group runs Paxos), so a crashed coordinator is replaced by its majority instead of waited for.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::08 Consensus (Raft & Paxos)
notes.front: How do Raft, Paxos and Zab avoid 2PC's single-coordinator blocking?
notes.back: Decisions need only a majority, and term/epoch numbers let a new leader supersede a failed one. Progress continues while a majority is up.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::08 Consensus (Raft & Paxos)
notes.front: What does a coordination service like ZooKeeper or etcd give applications?
notes.back: Consensus-backed primitives: leader election and locks with fencing tokens, failure detection, membership, small replicated metadata. Don't reimplement consensus yourself.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::09 Failure, Time & Fencing
notes.front: Why can't you tell whether a remote node is down?
notes.back: A missing reply could mean the request was lost, the node crashed or is slow, or the reply was lost. Timeouts are all you have: short ones cause false positives, long ones slow detection.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::09 Failure, Time & Fencing
notes.text: Failure models, mildest to worst: {{c1::crash-stop}} (halts forever), {{c2::crash-recovery}} (returns with stable storage intact), {{c3::omission}} (drops messages), {{c4::timing}} (responds too late), {{c5::Byzantine}} (arbitrary or malicious).
notes.extra: Raft/Paxos assume crash-recovery + omission with reliable disks.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::09 Failure, Time & Fencing
notes.front: What is a Byzantine fault, and do datacenter systems usually tolerate it?
notes.back: A node behaving arbitrarily or maliciously (lying, contradictory messages). Tolerating it is expensive (PBFT, 3f+1), so most systems assume nodes may crash or be slow but are honest.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::09 Failure, Time & Fencing
notes.front: Why are time-of-day clocks dangerous for ordering events across nodes?
notes.back: NTP-synced clocks drift and can jump backward; skew between nodes can exceed the gaps you measure. Ordering by them (e.g. LWW) silently loses data.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::09 Failure, Time & Fencing
notes.front: Monotonic clock vs time-of-day clock: when do you use which?
notes.back: Monotonic: measuring durations/timeouts on one node; never jumps back, but meaningless across nodes. Time-of-day: wall-clock timestamps; comparable-ish across nodes but can jump.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::09 Failure, Time & Fencing
notes.front: What do Lamport timestamps give you, and what can't they do?
notes.back: A (counter, node-ID) total order consistent with causality. They can't tell concurrent events from causally related ones, and the order is only known after the fact.
notes.extra: So they can't enforce uniqueness on the spot; that needs total order broadcast.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::09 Failure, Time & Fencing
notes.front: What can vector clocks detect that Lamport clocks can't?
notes.back: That two events are concurrent (neither vector ≤ the other), so conflicts can be surfaced instead of silently dropped (Dynamo). Cost: one counter per node.
notes.analogy: Each node keeps a scorecard of events seen from everyone; if neither scorecard dominates the other, the events happened independently.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::09 Failure, Time & Fencing
notes.front: What is a hybrid logical clock (HLC)?
notes.back: Physical time plus a logical counter: causally consistent like Lamport clocks but close to wall-clock time. Used by CockroachDB and YugabyteDB.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::09 Failure, Time & Fencing
notes.front: Fixed-timeout failure detector vs φ-accrual (Cassandra, Akka)?
notes.back: A fixed timeout picks one detection-speed/false-positive point for all conditions. φ-accrual learns heartbeat intervals and outputs a suspicion level; callers choose thresholds and it adapts to network latency.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::09 Failure, Time & Fencing
notes.front: What is a fencing token?
notes.back: A monotonically increasing number issued with each lock/lease grant. The protected resource rejects any request carrying a lower token than the highest it has seen.
notes.analogy: A deli ticket counter: once ticket 34 has been served, the clerk won't serve someone waving ticket 33.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::09 Failure, Time & Fencing
notes.front: A service holds a lease, hits a 30 s stop-the-world GC pause, and resumes. What goes wrong?
notes.back: No heartbeats during the pause → lease expires → another instance takes it and writes. The first wakes, unaware time passed, and keeps writing → two writers.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::09 Failure, Time & Fencing
notes.front: Why doesn't checking 'is the lock still mine?' right before writing make a lease safe?
notes.back: The pause can happen between the check and the write. Only a fencing token checked by the resource is sound, or operations that are harmless when run concurrently.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::09 Failure, Time & Fencing
notes.front: Why are leases vulnerable to clock drift and process pauses?
notes.back: A lease says 'leader until T'. A slow clock or a paused process (GC, VM migration, swap) makes local time say the lease is still valid while everyone else has moved on.
notes.analogy: A parking ticket 'valid until 15:00' only protects you if your watch agrees with the warden's.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::09 Failure, Time & Fencing
notes.front: How does Google Spanner's TrueTime deal with clock uncertainty?
notes.back: It returns an interval [earliest, latest] with bounded uncertainty (GPS/atomic clocks). A commit waits until 'latest' has passed, so timestamps are globally ordered.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::09 Failure, Time & Fencing
notes.front: What is split brain?
notes.back: Two nodes each believe they're the sole primary and both accept writes, producing divergent histories.
notes.analogy: Two captains on one ship, each giving orders after the radio between them failed.
notes.extra: Moving a virtual IP without fencing is the classic cause.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::09 Failure, Time & Fencing
notes.text: Preventing split brain: {{c1::quorum}} (only the majority side may act) plus {{c2::fencing}} (the old primary is blocked from writing, via fencing tokens or STONITH, 'shoot the other node in the head').

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::09 Failure, Time & Fencing
notes.front: 'fsyncgate': what did PostgreSQL learn about fsync, and what's the lesson for consensus?
notes.back: After a failed fsync, Linux may clear the dirty flag, so a retry 'succeeds' though data never hit disk. 'Persisted' can be silently false; on fsync failure, crash and recover.
notes.extra: PostgreSQL and etcd now panic on fsync errors.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::10 Resilience Patterns
notes.front: What is a gray failure?
notes.back: A component is degraded (slow, dropping some requests) yet passes its own health checks: the monitor and the clients see different things (differential observability).
notes.analogy: An employee who answers 'fine' at every check-in but quietly drops half their tickets.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::10 Resilience Patterns
notes.front: How do you detect gray failures?
notes.back: From the client's side: end-to-end canaries, load-balancer outlier ejection (Envoy, Istio), comparing each node's errors/latency with its peers. Health checks must exercise the real path.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::10 Resilience Patterns
notes.front: Why do naive retries turn a slow dependency into an outage?
notes.back: The dependency slows → callers time out and retry → load multiplies (3 retries = 4×) just when capacity is lowest. With retries at N layers, amplification is exponential.
notes.analogy: Everyone redialing a jammed phone line at once keeps it jammed.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::10 Resilience Patterns
notes.text: Taming retries: {{c1::exponential backoff with full jitter}}, {{c2::retry budgets}} (e.g. retries ≤ 10% of successful calls), and retrying at {{c3::only one layer}}, plus circuit breakers and load shedding.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::10 Resilience Patterns
notes.front: What is a metastable failure, and why doesn't removing the trigger fix it?
notes.back: A brief trigger pushes the system into a self-sustaining overload (retries ↑ → latency ↑ → retries ↑). The loop keeps going on its own; recovery needs actively shedding load below capacity.
notes.analogy: A traffic jam that persists long after the accident that caused it has been cleared.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::10 Resilience Patterns
notes.front: What is a thundering herd on cache expiry?
notes.back: A hot key expires and thousands of concurrent requests all miss and hit an origin sized only for cache-hit traffic.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::10 Resilience Patterns
notes.text: Thundering-herd mitigations: {{c1::request coalescing}} (singleflight: one origin fetch per key), {{c2::jittered TTLs / probabilistic early refresh}}, and {{c3::serve-stale-while-revalidate}}.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::10 Resilience Patterns
notes.front: What is static stability (AWS)?
notes.back: A system keeps working when a dependency, usually a control plane, fails, because it doesn't need to call it during the failure; it runs on state it already has.
notes.analogy: A ship that keeps sailing on its last heading when radio contact with shore is lost.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::10 Resilience Patterns
notes.front: Give examples of static stability in AWS and Kubernetes.
notes.back: EC2 instances keep running when the EC2 API is impaired; pre-provisioned capacity in each AZ avoids launching instances during an AZ outage; K8s pods and Services keep working when etcd is down.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::10 Resilience Patterns
notes.front: What design principle does Route 53 ARC (Paxos across 5 regions) illustrate?
notes.back: The failover mechanism must be more available than what it fails over. Never put the failover switch in the failing region's control plane.
notes.extra: 5 regions, majority of 3 needed, so one regional outage can't block failing out of it.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::10 Resilience Patterns
notes.front: What is shuffle sharding, and what does it buy?
notes.back: Give each customer a random subset of k of N nodes. Full overlap between two customers is rare, so one customer's poison requests hurt only a tiny fraction of others.
notes.analogy: Like dealing each player a random hand: two players almost never hold exactly the same cards.
notes.extra: 8 nodes, k=2: only 1 in 28 customer pairs share both nodes.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::10 Resilience Patterns
notes.front: What is a cell-based architecture, and why does it sidestep CAP-style trade-offs?
notes.back: Many independent, fixed-size full-stack cells sharing no state, with a thin router mapping customers to cells. No cross-cell coordination; failures stay inside one cell.
notes.analogy: Watertight compartments in a ship's hull: a breach floods one compartment, not the ship.
notes.extra: Hard parts: the routing layer and moving customers between cells.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::10 Resilience Patterns
notes.front: Why do AWS and Azure roll changes out one AZ/region at a time?
notes.back: Bad deploys and config pushes are correlated failures, the top cause of big outages, hitting everything at once. Waves with bake time turn them into bounded, reversible ones.
notes.extra: K8s analogue: maxUnavailable, progressive delivery.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::11 Messaging, Streams & Batch
notes.front: Two Generals: why is exactly-once delivery impossible over a lossy network?
notes.back: Every acknowledgement can be lost too, so neither side can ever be sure the other knows. Real systems do at-least-once delivery + idempotent processing and call that 'exactly-once'.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::11 Messaging, Streams & Batch
notes.text: Delivery semantics: {{c1::at-most-once}} (send once, never retry: may lose); {{c2::at-least-once}} (retry until acked: may duplicate); 'exactly-once processing' = at-least-once + {{c3::an idempotent or deduplicating consumer}}.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::11 Messaging, Streams & Batch
notes.front: Where must deduplication live for exactly-once effects?
notes.back: At the consumer / state owner, keyed by a client-chosen ID, with the dedup record committed atomically with the effect.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::11 Messaging, Streams & Batch
notes.front: Why is idempotence central to reliable data pipelines?
notes.back: Failures cause retries, so operations must be safe to apply twice. Idempotence plus dedup (operation ID, offset) gives exactly-once effects on at-least-once delivery.
notes.analogy: Pressing a lift call button five times still calls one lift.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::11 Messaging, Streams & Batch
notes.front: How do idempotency tokens (EC2 ClientToken, Stripe keys) work?
notes.back: The client sends the same unique token on every retry; the service stores token → result and returns the stored result for duplicates.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::11 Messaging, Streams & Batch
notes.front: What is the end-to-end argument for correctness?
notes.back: Some guarantees (e.g. true duplicate suppression) can only be done at the application endpoints. TCP retransmits or DB transactions alone can't; you need end-to-end operation IDs.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::11 Messaging, Streams & Batch
notes.front: Amazon SQS Standard vs FIFO?
notes.back: Standard: at-least-once, best-effort order, near-unlimited throughput. FIFO: order per MessageGroupId; 'exactly-once' = dedup by ID within a 5-minute window.
notes.extra: Consumers must still be idempotent beyond the window or after mid-processing crashes.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::11 Messaging, Streams & Batch
notes.front: AMQP/JMS-style brokers vs log-based brokers (Kafka)?
notes.back: AMQP/JMS: messages deleted once acked; good task queues, hard to replay. Log-based: durable partitioned log; consumers track an offset, so they can replay and read independently.
notes.analogy: A to-do list where items are crossed off vs a diary that each reader works through with their own bookmark.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::11 Messaging, Streams & Batch
notes.front: What is change data capture (CDC)?
notes.back: Turning a database's stream of writes into an event feed for other systems (search, caches, warehouses). The DB stays the system of record; downstream stores are derived.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::11 Messaging, Streams & Batch
notes.front: Event sourcing vs CDC?
notes.back: Event sourcing: the app stores immutable domain events as the source of truth and derives state by replay. CDC: extracts low-level row changes from a normal database.
notes.analogy: A bank statement listing every transaction vs only the balance: you can always recompute the balance from the statement.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::11 Messaging, Streams & Batch
notes.front: Event time vs processing time: why does it matter?
notes.back: Event time: when it happened. Processing time: when the engine sees it. Delays and out-of-order arrival make them diverge, so windowing by processing time gives wrong results.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::11 Messaging, Streams & Batch
notes.front: What is a watermark in stream processing?
notes.back: The engine's claim that no events older than T will still arrive, letting windows close and emit. Events later than the allowed lateness are dropped or sent to a side output.
notes.analogy: A teacher announcing 'no more exam papers after this', accepting that a rare latecomer will be turned away.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::11 Messaging, Streams & Batch
notes.text: Stream windows: {{c1::tumbling}} (fixed size, non-overlapping), {{c2::hopping}} (fixed size, overlapping by a step), {{c3::sliding}} (all events within an interval of each other), {{c4::session}} (closed by a gap of inactivity).

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::11 Messaging, Streams & Batch
notes.front: How do stream processors get exactly-once effects?
notes.back: Checkpoint operator state (Flink) or microbatch (Spark Streaming), combined with idempotent or transactional output, so replayed messages don't double-apply.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::11 Messaging, Streams & Batch
notes.front: What is the MapReduce model?
notes.back: Map each record to key-value pairs → the framework sorts and groups by key (shuffle) → reduce all values per key. Inputs and outputs are immutable files on a distributed FS.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::11 Messaging, Streams & Batch
notes.text: Batch joins: {{c1::sort-merge join}} (both sides sorted by key, merged in the reducer); {{c2::broadcast hash join}} (small side loaded into memory on every mapper); {{c3::partitioned hash join}} (both sides partitioned the same way, joined per partition).

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::11 Messaging, Streams & Batch
notes.front: Why are dataflow engines (Spark, Flink) faster than MapReduce for multi-stage jobs?
notes.back: They plan the whole job as one graph, so they pipeline operators instead of writing every intermediate step to disk, keep data in memory, and skip unnecessary sorts.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::11 Messaging, Streams & Batch
notes.front: Why is the immutable-input design of batch jobs valuable?
notes.back: Inputs never change, so jobs are deterministic and retryable: re-run to debug, keep old output to roll back, experiment safely. Derived data becomes reproducible.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::11 Messaging, Streams & Batch
notes.front: What does 'unbundling the database' mean?
notes.back: Compose specialized systems (storage, indexes, caches, search, stream processors) connected by logs instead of one monolithic DB. The log keeps all derived views consistent.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::11 Messaging, Streams & Batch
notes.front: What is the lambda architecture?
notes.back: A batch layer for accurate, reprocessable results plus a stream layer for fast approximate results, merged at read time.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::11 Messaging, Streams & Batch
notes.front: What's the main critique of the lambda architecture, and the alternative?
notes.back: The same logic lives in two systems, which is costly and error-prone. A stream processor that can reprocess history (Kafka + Flink, 'kappa') does both.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::11 Messaging, Streams & Batch
notes.front: What is CQRS in DDIA's framing?
notes.back: Separate the write path (commands/events appended to a log) from the read path (query-optimized views derived from it). You can rebuild or add views by replaying the log.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::12 Cloud & Kubernetes Case Studies
notes.front: What is etcd's role in Kubernetes, and which protocol does it run?
notes.back: etcd runs Raft and is the only stateful control-plane component: every object is a key under /registry/. kube-apiserver is a stateless front end over it.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::12 Cloud & Kubernetes Case Studies
notes.front: What does the Kubernetes control plane inherit from etcd's Raft?
notes.back: CP behaviour, majority-quorum availability, and write latency of at least one fsync plus one majority round trip.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::12 Cloud & Kubernetes Case Studies
notes.front: Why run etcd with 3 or 5 members, never 4 or 6?
notes.back: Fault tolerance = ⌊(N−1)/2⌋. Four tolerates 1 failure like three, but has a bigger quorum (slower writes) and one more machine that can fail. Five tolerates 2.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::12 Cloud & Kubernetes Case Studies
notes.front: A 3-member etcd cluster across 2 AZs (2+1) vs 3 AZs (1+1+1)?
notes.back: 3 AZs: any one AZ loss leaves 2/3, quorum intact. 2 AZs: losing the AZ with 2 members leaves 1/3, no quorum. Rule: no single failure domain may hold a majority.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::12 Cloud & Kubernetes Case Studies
notes.front: Why is etcd write latency bounded below by disk fsync?
notes.back: Each Raft entry must be fsynced to the WAL on a majority before the ack, or a crash could lose a 'committed' entry.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::12 Cloud & Kubernetes Case Studies
notes.front: How do slow disks show up in etcd, and what do you monitor?
notes.back: As leader elections and apiserver timeouts, not disk errors. Use dedicated low-latency SSDs; keep wal_fsync_duration_seconds p99 under ~10 ms.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::12 Cloud & Kubernetes Case Studies
notes.front: etcd linearizable vs serializable reads?
notes.back: Linearizable (default): goes through ReadIndex; reflects every write committed before the read. Serializable: served from the local member; can be stale on a partitioned member.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::12 Cloud & Kubernetes Case Studies
notes.front: How can kube-apiserver serve consistent reads from its watch cache?
notes.back: It uses etcd progress notifications to confirm the cache has reached the current revision before answering: ReadIndex at the cache layer.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::12 Cloud & Kubernetes Case Studies
notes.front: How does the Kubernetes API do optimistic concurrency?
notes.back: Each object carries metadata.resourceVersion (etcd revision). Updates must send the version they read; the apiserver compare-and-swaps and returns 409 Conflict if it changed.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::12 Cloud & Kubernetes Case Studies
notes.front: What does the lack of cross-object transactions in the K8s API force controllers to do?
notes.back: Re-read and retry on conflict (RetryOnConflict) and make every multi-step operation idempotent and reconciled, never assumed atomic.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::12 Cloud & Kubernetes Case Studies
notes.front: In Kubernetes, how do you do 'create A, then B, roll back if B fails'?
notes.back: You don't roll back, you reconcile: write desired state and let a controller converge idempotently. Use ownerReferences for GC, finalizers for teardown, status.conditions for progress.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::12 Cloud & Kubernetes Case Studies
notes.front: Why are Kubernetes controllers level-triggered rather than edge-triggered?
notes.back: Acting on each event breaks permanently if one is missed (watch drop, restart, 410 Gone). Comparing current with desired state converges from any starting point; watches are just a latency optimization.
notes.analogy: A thermostat reads the current temperature rather than counting how often the door was opened.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::12 Cloud & Kubernetes Case Studies
notes.front: How do kube-scheduler / controller-manager replicas elect a leader?
notes.back: Compare-and-swap on a Lease object (coordination.k8s.io). Defaults: leaseDuration 15 s, renewDeadline 10 s, retryPeriod 2 s.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::12 Cloud & Kubernetes Case Studies
notes.front: Why is Kubernetes Lease-based leader election not consensus?
notes.back: Leadership is time-based: a paused leader may still act after its lease expired and a new leader started. It's safe only for actions that are idempotent or guarded by resourceVersion.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::12 Cloud & Kubernetes Case Studies
notes.front: Why does Kubernetes wait minutes before evicting pods from an unreachable node?
notes.back: Timeout-based detection can't tell a partitioned kubelet from a dead one. Acting slowly trades availability for not running workloads twice.
notes.extra: Node NotReady after ~40–50 s without Lease renewal; eviction after tolerationSeconds (300 s).

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::12 Cloud & Kubernetes Case Studies
notes.front: Why won't a StatefulSet recreate a pod from an unreachable node until the old one is confirmed deleted?
notes.back: It promises at most one pod per identity. The old pod may still be running and writing; a second pod-0 would be split brain on the same volume.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::12 Cloud & Kubernetes Case Studies
notes.front: What does force-deleting a StatefulSet pod (--grace-period=0 --force) mean in distributed-systems terms?
notes.back: A human acting as the fence: asserting the node is really dead. Cloud providers automate it by deleting the Node when the instance is terminated.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::12 Cloud & Kubernetes Case Studies
notes.front: What does a 410 Gone on an etcd watch mean, and what's the lesson?
notes.back: The requested revision was compacted (apiserver compacts every 5 min), so the client must relist. Any replicated log gets truncated; consumers must be able to rebuild from a snapshot.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::12 Cloud & Kubernetes Case Studies
notes.front: What happens to Kubernetes when etcd hits its space quota?
notes.back: A NOSPACE alarm makes etcd read-only: all writes fail, pods keep running but nothing can be scheduled or changed. Fix: compact → defrag → disarm alarm.
notes.extra: Default quota 2 GB, max recommended 8 GB. Causes: Events/Jobs/CR growth, missing compaction.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::12 Cloud & Kubernetes Case Studies
notes.front: What happens to a Kubernetes cluster when etcd loses quorum?
notes.back: The control plane stops (no scheduling, scaling, rollouts, Lease renewals), but the data plane stays up: running pods, Service routing and DNS keep working.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::12 Cloud & Kubernetes Case Studies
notes.front: How should a PodDisruptionBudget be set for etcd, ZooKeeper or Kafka KRaft, and what doesn't it cover?
notes.back: maxUnavailable: 1 (or minAvailable = quorum) so drains never drop below majority. PDBs cover only voluntary evictions; add topology spread for AZ outages.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::12 Cloud & Kubernetes Case Studies
notes.front: How is a single DynamoDB partition replicated?
notes.back: Three replicas in three AZs; a Paxos-elected leader takes writes and acks once 2 of 3 have persisted.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::12 Cloud & Kubernetes Case Studies
notes.front: DynamoDB eventually consistent vs strongly consistent reads?
notes.back: Eventual (default, half the RCU): any replica, may miss a just-committed write. Strong: served by the leader, sees all prior writes. Not available on GSIs.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::12 Cloud & Kubernetes Case Studies
notes.front: DynamoDB Global Tables (default): consistency model and conflict resolution?
notes.back: Multi-active, asynchronous cross-region replication (~1 s), conflicts resolved by last-writer-wins: concurrent writes in two regions silently drop one. PA/EL.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::12 Cloud & Kubernetes Case Studies
notes.front: What do DynamoDB multi-Region strong consistency tables trade?
notes.back: Writes go through a cross-region quorum: linearizability at the cost of cross-region write latency. PACELC as a per-table choice.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::12 Cloud & Kubernetes Case Studies
notes.front: How does DynamoDB TransactWriteItems get atomicity across partitions, and at what cost?
notes.back: A durable coordinator runs 2PC across partition leaders. Cost: 2× WCU per item, more latency, and TransactionConflict rejections. Use only where needed.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::12 Cloud & Kubernetes Case Studies
notes.front: What consistency does Amazon S3 give since December 2020, and how?
notes.back: Strong read-after-write for all GETs and LISTs, including overwrites and deletes, at no extra cost. The metadata cache layer was made coherently versioned, so stale entries are detected.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::12 Cloud & Kubernetes Case Studies
notes.front: Amazon Aurora storage quorums: what are they, and why 6 copies?
notes.back: 6 copies over 3 AZs; write 4/6, read 3/6. Survives an AZ loss with writes intact (4 left) and AZ + 1 more failure with reads intact (3 left).

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::12 Cloud & Kubernetes Case Studies
notes.front: Why is Aurora's storage layer described as 'the log is the database'?
notes.back: The engine ships only redo log records to storage nodes, which materialize pages themselves: far less replication traffic, fast failover, replicas sharing one volume.
notes.extra: Azure analogue: Azure SQL Hyperscale (page servers + log service).

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::12 Cloud & Kubernetes Case Studies
notes.front: Aurora Multi-AZ vs Aurora Global Database on CAP/PACELC?
notes.back: In-region: synchronous 4/6 quorum, CP. Global: async storage replication (<1 s), stale secondary reads (EL); failover loses up to the lag, so RPO = staleness.
notes.extra: Always ask: consistent within which boundary?

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::12 Cloud & Kubernetes Case Studies
notes.front: RDS Multi-AZ fails over by flipping DNS. What client-side failure does that cause?
notes.back: Clients with cached DNS (JVM defaults) or long-lived pooled connections keep talking to the old primary or hang. Fix: honour TTL, cap connection lifetime, or use RDS Proxy.
notes.extra: A failover that requires clients to notice is only half a failover.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::12 Cloud & Kubernetes Case Studies
notes.front: How can Route 53 offer a 100% availability SLA without breaking CAP?
notes.back: The SLA covers the data plane (answering queries): massively replicated, possibly stale, AP. Changing records is a separate, eventually propagated control plane.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::12 Cloud & Kubernetes Case Studies
notes.text: Cosmos DB consistency levels, strongest to weakest: {{c1::strong}} → {{c2::bounded staleness}} → {{c3::session}} (the default) → {{c4::consistent prefix}} → {{c5::eventual}}.
notes.extra: Weaker levels: lower latency, fewer RUs, higher multi-region availability.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::12 Cloud & Kubernetes Case Studies
notes.front: What does Cosmos DB bounded staleness guarantee?
notes.back: Reads lag writes by at most K versions or T time, whichever comes first: quantified staleness instead of a strong/eventual binary. Single-region, it behaves like strong.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::12 Cloud & Kubernetes Case Studies
notes.front: How is Cosmos DB session consistency implemented?
notes.back: The SDK carries a session token (per-partition sequence numbers); a replica serves the read only once it has caught up to that token.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::12 Cloud & Kubernetes Case Studies
notes.front: What silently breaks Cosmos DB session consistency?
notes.back: Not passing the session token along: multiple service instances, a function per request, or a web tier that doesn't return it to the browser. Read-your-writes becomes eventual.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::12 Cloud & Kubernetes Case Studies
notes.front: Cosmos DB strong consistency across regions: what does a write cost, and what's incompatible?
notes.back: Synchronous commit to a majority of regions, ≈ 2× RTT to the farthest region. Incompatible with multi-region writes: no linearizability with independent concurrent writers.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::12 Cloud & Kubernetes Case Studies
notes.text: Cosmos DB multi-region write conflict policies: {{c1::last-writer-wins}} (default, on _ts), {{c2::custom stored procedure}} (server-side merge), {{c3::manual}} (conflicts feed for the app).
notes.extra: If losing a write is unacceptable, model updates to commute (counters, sets) or use single-region writes.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::12 Cloud & Kubernetes Case Studies
notes.front: How does Cosmos DB replicate inside a region?
notes.back: Each physical partition is a 4-replica set; a write is durable at a majority (3/4). Strong/bounded reads use a majority; session/eventual read a single replica.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::12 Cloud & Kubernetes Case Studies
notes.text: Azure Storage redundancy: {{c1::LRS}} = 3 sync copies in one datacenter; {{c2::ZRS}} = 3 sync copies across 3 AZs; {{c3::GRS}} = LRS + async copy to the paired region; {{c4::RA-GRS}} = GRS with readable (stale) secondary.
notes.extra: Geo-failover loses writes not yet replicated (RPO typically < 15 min).

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::12 Cloud & Kubernetes Case Studies
notes.front: Why is Azure Storage strongly consistent within a region?
notes.back: Each key range is served by one partition server; the stream layer replicates extents synchronously in a chain (acked when all 3 persist), with Paxos for extent metadata.
notes.extra: Exposes ETags for optimistic concurrency.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::12 Cloud & Kubernetes Case Studies
notes.front: Azure Service Fabric stateful services: what is quorum loss?
notes.back: When fewer than a majority of a partition's replicas are up, writes are refused (reads may continue) until replicas return or an operator forces a possibly lossy recovery.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::12 Cloud & Kubernetes Case Studies
notes.front: Using Azure Blob leases for leader election: failure mode and fix?
notes.back: The holder pauses, the lease expires, another instance takes over, the old one resumes as 'leader'. Fix: fence writes with conditional ETag (If-Match) or an epoch.

notes.deck: Distributed Systems & Data::12 Cloud & Kubernetes Case Studies
notes.front: Azure SQL failover groups: replication mode, and what must the app handle?
notes.back: Async geo-replication: an unplanned failover can lose recent commits. Apps must use the listener endpoint, retry transient errors, and accept stale reads from the secondary.
